claims.text: Percolation of SRO clusters in single-phase bcc HfNbTaTiZr will produce a non-monotonic increase, or reduced suppression, of thermal conductivity relative to a random solid solution.
A percolative network of coherent SRO interfaces suppresses phonon scattering more effectively than isolated SRO clusters.
The proposed effect requires a potential energy surface that captures the enthalpic cost of disrupting local chemical order.
HfNbTaTiZr has thermal conductivity in the range 10–17 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
The low thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr is associated with lattice distortion and defects that impede electron and phonon propagation.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr state is a single-phase bcc random solid solution or contains only isolated SRO clusters.
Annealing below the order-disorder transition temperature can create a percolating SRO network in HfNbTaTiZr.
Formation or disruption of local order can carry an additional DAPB-like energy cost in a bcc refractory high-entropy alloy.
SRO is thermodynamically stable without second-phase formation in single-phase bcc HfNbTaTiZr over approximately 800–1500 K.
Phonon transport is the dominant heat-transfer mechanism under the proposed conditions.
A continuous SRO network acts as a coherent interface network analogous to diffuse antiphase boundaries and changes phonon mean free paths differently from isolated scattering centers.
Isolated SRO clusters typically increase phonon scattering and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolation of SRO can establish a distinct phononic-band or coherent-interface regime in which scattering cross-section per unit volume decreases because disorder is spatially correlated.
SRO flattens the energy landscape for edge dislocations in MoNbTaW and thereby reduces solute drag and enhances edge-dislocation mobility.
The SRO-induced flattening of the edge-dislocation energy landscape can extend to phonon modes and reduce their effective scattering potential.
Crossing the SRO percolation threshold will cause an inflection or other deviation from serial, parallel, or effective-medium mixing predictions.
The percolated SRO state will have higher thermal conductivity than the random solid solution at the same temperature.
Standard mixing models assume additive scattering contributions and do not capture the proposed percolative conductivity change.
Transformation of coherent SRO clusters into a distinct Laves or B2 second phase would introduce interfaces and likely reduce thermal conductivity further.
Existing literature on fcc systems indicates that SRO reduces thermal conductivity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows merely a 'reduced suppression' relative to the random solid solution, which could still leave conductivity below the random-state value, whereas the predicted outcome unconditionally states that conductivity will be higher than the random solid solution.
